content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato (batata) is a starchy root vegetable rich in carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals. Boiling retains most nutrients, giving it a soft texture and a mildly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potato belongs to the Convolvulaceae family and is not related to regular potato.
It is high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Around the world batata is prepared in many ways: boiled, baked, fried, and used in desserts.
Several cultivars exist with flesh ranging from white to bright orange and purple.
Batata was domesticated in Central and South America over 5,000 years ago.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: The orange flesh provides a high amount of provitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates supply steady energy and promote satiety.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and supports gut microbiome health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sweet potato provides vitamin B6, thiamine, and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Potassium, magnesium, and iron in sweet potato contribute to heart and muscle function.

items.title: High glycemic index after boiling
items.content: Boiled sweet potato can raise blood glucose quickly, so people with diabetes should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to sweet potato.

items.title: Skin considerations
items.content: If the skin is left on, pesticide residues may remain; wash thoroughly before cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled sweet potato can be eaten on its own, added to salads, soups, mashed, or used as a filling for wraps. Cut into cubes for quick snacks or blend into smoothies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store boiled sweet potato in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze portioned pieces—they retain flavor and nutrients.
